_comment: The source corpus is tokenized with contractions split apart — it holds
"don" + "'t" and "i" + "'m", so "don't" and "i'm" appear NOWHERE in the
raw list, while the bare clitics ('s, 't, 'm, 're) rank in the top 15.
Prediction without contractions is useless for real writing, so we add them
back here.
Counts are hand-set on the same scale as the corpus (for reference: is =
7.4M, do = 4.4M, not = 4.3M, are = 4.2M, will = 2.0M, would = 1.3M) to place
each contraction at roughly its true conversational rank. They are estimates
and do not need to be exact — getting "won't" and "wouldn't" in the wrong
order by a few ranks has no observable effect on suggestions.
dropRaw removes two kinds of debris. First, the apostrophe-less spellings
the corpus picked up from sloppy subtitles ('dont', 'youre'), which would
otherwise be offered as suggestions and look like bugs. Second, the orphaned
STEMS left behind by the same tokenizer split: dropping "don't" into "don"
+ "'t" leaves 'don' sitting at rank 31 and 'doesn' at 208, so typing "do"
suggests 'don' and 'doesn' above real words.
Both lists cover ONLY unambiguous debris. Real words that happen to look
like debris stay: 'won', 'can' and 'haven' are stems of won't/can't/haven't
but are also ordinary English, and 'ill', 'well', 'were', 'its', 'shed',
'wed', 'lets' and 'id' are real words — 'ill' especially, which an AAC user
needs. ('haven' keeps an inflated rank as a result; a rare word placing a
little too high is a far smaller wart than a missing one.)
